claims.text: Degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 at high temperature is governed by competition between protective Al/Cr oxidation and non-protective Co/Ti oxidation.
Selective oxidation of Al and Cr produces a partially protective inner Al2O3/Cr2O3 scale in oxidizing environments.
Co- and Ti-rich oxides are non-protective and disrupt the Al2O3/Cr2O3 scale.
Local discontinuities caused by Co- and Ti-rich oxides lead to eventual degradation.
Low oxygen availability in reducing environments suppresses formation of the protective scale.
Suppression of the protective scale in reducing environments accelerates internal oxidation and weakens oxide adhesion.
The starting alloy is homogeneous and has an fcc structure with uniformly distributed Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti.
The starting alloy has high strength and fatigue resistance.
The starting alloy has no preexisting oxide layers.
Coupons will be exposed at approximately 900 °C for up to 100 hours in oxidizing and reducing atmospheres.
Oxide-scale continuity and adhesion mediate degradation of the alloy.
Al and Cr oxidize more slowly than Co and Ti and form stable protective oxides.
Co and Ti oxidize rapidly and form volatile or less-adherent oxides.
Competition among the constituent oxidation reactions creates a dual-layered or segmented scale.
Thermal stresses and interfacial mismatches between oxide regions cause microcracking and scale spallation.
Microcracking and scale spallation accelerate degradation.
Reducing atmospheres will produce more internal oxidation and a higher overall degradation rate than oxidizing atmospheres.
The proposed mechanism applies around 900 °C in strongly oxidizing or reducing atmospheres, while substantially lower temperatures or intermediate oxygen potentials may change the behavior.

The hypothesis would be falsified if both atmospheres produce a continuous, adherent, uniform Al2O3/Cr2O3 scale without significant Co/Ti interference and without a significant difference in degradation rate.
